title: Milestone: Two Families of Faith
objective: After this level you can compare the Abrahamic and Indian traditions: one life and a final judgment, or many lives and release from rebirth.
summary: Traditional Judaism, Christianity and Islam look to one lifetime, resurrection and a Last Judgment; the Indian family sees many lives, karma and release.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Two families of faith, one big question.
cards.body: What comes after this life? Level 8 sorted religions into families. Now, with Hindus and Jains met up close, set the Abrahamic and Indian families side by side and watch their answers diverge.

items.label: Abrahamic family
points: Traditionally one lifetime, then resurrection and a Last Judgment

items.label: Indian family
points: Many lives in samsara, shaped by karma
The hope is release (moksha) from rebirth
Time turns in cycles of destruction and renewal

cards.headline: Many voices on each side
cards.body: Neither side is one voice. Muslims believe in a Day of Judgement, when every human life will be assessed. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead. Maimonides counted resurrection of the dead among his 13 principles of Jewish faith, though Jews have long debated it. In both families your actions reach beyond this life: weighed at a final judgment, or carried forward by karma.

cards.headline: Milestone: two families compared
learned: How karma, rebirth and moksha fit together, and why release is the ultimate aim for many Hindus.
Why Hinduism is called a family of traditions, from the Upanishads to Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess.
What Jains mean by ahimsa, and how monks, nuns and laypeople keep their five vows.
How the Abrahamic and Indian families answer what comes after this life.

questions.prompt: The word "Hindu" began as the name of what?

options.label: A founding teacher
A river, the Indus
A holy mountain
A royal dynasty

questions.explanation: Hindu comes from Sindhu, the Sanskrit name for the river Indus.

questions.prompt: In the Chandogya Upanishad, what does salt dissolved in water teach about the self?

options.label: That it can be seen by anyone who looks
That it disappears when the body dies
options.rationale: The salt is still there, tasted throughout.

options.label: That it is unseen, yet present throughout
That it belongs only to priests
options.rationale: Uddalaka tells his son, "you are that".

questions.explanation: Like salt in water, the self is unseen yet present throughout.

questions.prompt: Which three paths does Krishna teach in the Bhagavad Gita?

options.label: Action, knowledge and devotion
Fasting, pilgrimage and charity
options.rationale: Those aren't the Gita's three paths.

options.label: Sacrifice, chant and study
options.rationale: Those belong to Vedic ritual, not the Gita's paths.

options.label: Truth, non-stealing and non-violence
options.rationale: Those are among the Jain vows.

questions.prompt: Why is darshan described as working both ways?

options.label: The deity and the worshipper exchange gifts of food
options.rationale: Food offerings are part of puja, not the meaning of darshan.

options.label: Two priests look at the image together
The worshipper sees the deity and is blessed by being seen
It happens once at home and once at a temple
options.rationale: Darshan can happen anywhere the deity is beheld.

questions.explanation: In darshan the worshipper beholds the deity and receives a blessing by being seen.

questions.prompt: Why is ahimsa, non-violence, the heart of Jain teaching?

options.label: Jains believe violence angers a creator god
options.rationale: The reason is souls and karma.

options.label: Jains believe every being has a soul, and harm binds karma to one's own
Ahimsa is a law passed by Mahavira's father
options.rationale: He left the palace; ahimsa is a teaching.

options.label: Jains avoid harm only on festival days

questions.explanation: Every living thing has a soul, and harming others attracts karma, so protecting others protects your own soul.

questions.prompt: Which pairing matches each family's traditional view?

options.label: Abrahamic: many lives. Indian: one life and a final judgment
Abrahamic: one lifetime and a Last Judgment. Indian: many lives and release
Both: one lifetime followed by rebirth as an animal
Both: time repeats in endless cycles
options.rationale: The Abrahamic view looks to an end of history.

questions.explanation: Traditional Judaism, Christianity and Islam hold to one lifetime and a Last Judgment; the Indian family sees samsara and hopes for release.

questions.prompt: A Muslim and a Hindu both believe actions matter beyond this life. How does each picture that?

options.label: Both expect actions to be weighed at the Day of Judgement
Both expect karma to shape their next birth
Neither thinks actions matter after death
The Muslim, judgment of one life; the Hindu, karma carried into lives to come

questions.explanation: Muslims believe every life is assessed on the Day of Judgement; Hindus believe karma carries actions forward through rebirth.
